Cost‑effectiveness analyses published in 2023–24 suggest that semaglutide can be cost‑effective at willingness‑to‑pay thresholds of $50,000–$100,000 per quality‑adjusted life year (QALY) when used in patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m² or BMI ≥30 kg/m² plus comorbidities. 1. **BMI Thresholds and Comorbidity Requirement**  
   • Initiate therapy only in adults with BMI ≥30 kg/m² or BMI ≥27 kg/m² plus at least one of the following: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, or osteoarthritis.  
   • For patients with BMI 25–29.9 kg/m², require documented weight‑related comorbidities and a prior failure of lifestyle intervention.

   • Require at least 6 months of supervised lifestyle modification (dietary counseling, structured exercise program, behavioral therapy) documented in the medical record.  
   • Document trial of at least one FDA‑approved weight‑loss medication (e.g., phentermine/topiramate, naltrexone/bupropion) or a non‑pharmacologic intervention that failed to achieve ≥5 % weight loss.

   • Baseline labs: fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipid panel, liver function tests, thyroid‑stimulating hormone (TSH), and serum creatinine.  
   • Imaging or endoscopy is not routinely required unless clinically indicated for pancreatitis risk assessment.

   • Schedule follow‑up visits at 3, 6, and 12 months to assess weight trajectory, adherence, and adverse events.  
   • Require documentation of ≥5 % weight loss by month 6 as a continuation criterion; otherwise consider therapy discontinuation or switch.

   • Implement prior‑authorization with a standardized electronic form capturing BMI, comorbidities, prior therapies, and baseline labs.

Routine laboratory monitoring for liver enzymes at baseline and every 3 months can detect drug‑induced hepatotoxicity early. For patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, contraindications should preclude therapy.

Under ERISA, self‑insured plans may set coverage policies that differ from commercial insurers, provided they are applied uniformly and not discriminatory. My training data extend to mid‑2024. Since then, there have been reports of significant price reductions for semaglutide due to manufacturer rebates, as well as preliminary pricing announcements for tirzepatide that could shift cost‑effectiveness thresholds. Emerging guidelines from the ADA and AACE in 2025–26 may refine BMI thresholds or expand indications to include patients with BMI ≥25 kg/m² without comorbidities. Moreover, ERISA interpretations regarding “reasonable medical necessity” for obesity pharmacotherapy have evolved in a few appellate decisions post‑2024, potentially affecting coverage determinations.
